intro: Every society has ideas about who does what work, who gives orders and who must bow. In this unit you will visit India, China, Japan and Korea. In each place, people were sorted into groups by birth, by learning or by the sword. Those groups shaped where people lived, whom they married and how they spoke to one another.

You will also meet people who questioned these orders. A Dalit boy who sat on a sack at school grew up to help write India's Constitution. Poets sang that God looks at the heart, not at birth. Japanese reformers, many of them samurai, ended their own class. Korean scholars made an alphabet so ordinary people could read.

By the end, you will be able to explain how varna and jati differ, how exams and birth decided rank in East Asia, and how laws and movements changed these systems. You will weigh different views fairly and back up your ideas with facts from the unit.
bigQuestion: How did Asian societies rank people, and how did people inside those systems work to change them?

timeline.t: Hymns later gathered in the Rig Veda are composed in northern India
The Buddha and Confucius teach in India and China
China's Sui dynasty begins choosing officials by written exams
The Joseon dynasty begins in Korea, led by a yangban elite
King Sejong publishes the Hangul alphabet for ordinary Koreans
Tokugawa Ieyasu becomes shogun of Japan
The Meiji Restoration begins to end Japan's samurai class
Korea's Gabo Reforms officially end class distinctions and slavery
Ambedkar leads the Mahad protest for Dalits' right to public water
India's Constitution comes into force and abolishes untouchability
Ambedkar and many followers become Buddhists in Nagpur

words.d: one of four broad social groups described in ancient Hindu texts
a local birth group, often tied to a kind of work and to marriage inside the group
a name many people once called untouchable chose for themselves; it means broken or crushed
loving devotion to God; a movement teaching that anyone could reach God
a country's highest set of laws, describing the government and people's rights
in India, seats in schools, jobs and legislatures set aside for groups held back by caste
a written test used in imperial China to choose government officials
the ability of people to move up or down in wealth or rank
the top military ruler of Japan, who held real power while the emperor reigned in name
the hereditary warrior class of Japan, ranked at the top of the Tokugawa order
the 1868 change that ended the shogun's rule and began Japan's rapid reforms
the educated, land-holding elite of Joseon Korea, from whom most officials came

test.q: What is the main difference between varna and jati?
choices: Varna is a four-part idea in texts; jati is a local birth group
Varna is Japanese; jati is Korean
Varna is a law; jati is a religion
They mean exactly the same thing
test.why: Varna is the broad four-group idea; jati is the birth group of daily life.

test.q: Which leader chaired the committee that drafted India's Constitution?
Which teaching challenged caste by saying actions, not birth, make a person noble?
choices: The Rig Veda hymn of the cosmic body
test.why: The Buddha taught that a person becomes noble by good actions.

test.q: What does Article 17 of India's Constitution do?
test.why: Article 17 abolishes untouchability and forbids it in any form.

test.q: Which statement about reservations is balanced?
choices: Supporters say they opened doors; critics prefer merit or income
Everyone in India agrees they are perfect
test.why: The unit gives both the supporters' and critics' views.

test.q: What was the Sikh langar meant to show?
choices: That all people are equal before God
test.why: At the langar everyone eats together, showing equality.

test.q: In imperial China, what was the main path to becoming an official?
test.why: China chose many officials through civil-service exams.

test.q: Why did the exams give only limited social mobility?
choices: They were given once a century
Preparing took years and money that poor families lacked
test.why: Wealthy families could pay for tutors and long years of study.

test.q: Who stood at the top of the Tokugawa four-rank order?
test.why: Japan put the hereditary samurai at the top.

test.q: Why could a rich Edo merchant still have to bow to a poor samurai?
choices: Official rank mattered more than wealth
test.why: Under Tokugawa rules, rank came from birth, not money.

test.q: What did the alternate-attendance rule do?
choices: Made lords spend every other year in Edo
test.why: Lords had to live in Edo every other year, which kept them loyal.

test.q: Which reform took away the samurai's special role as fighters?
test.why: Conscription drafted men of every class into the army.

test.q: What was the Satsuma Rebellion of 1877?
test.why: Saigo Takamori led it, and the new conscript army defeated it.

test.q: Which group formed Joseon Korea's elite?
test.why: The yangban held land and most government offices.

test.q: What do Ambedkar's Mahad protest and King Sejong's Hangul have in common?
choices: Both opened something to people who had been shut out
test.why: Mahad opened public water to Dalits; Hangul opened reading to ordinary Koreans.

write.prompt: Which did more to change a system of rank: new laws from the government, or movements led by people inside the system? Choose two societies from this unit. Use two or three facts or sources to support your claim.
tips: Name your examples, such as Article 17, the Mahad protest or the Meiji conscription law.
Give the other side fairly before you explain your claim.
Use unit terms such as jati, reservations, samurai and yangban.
Remember that a law and a change in daily life are not always the same thing.
